newsitem.title: USA: Conoco, Reading & Bates in $400 million venture.
newsitem.headline: Conoco, Reading & Bates in $400 million venture.

text.p: Conoco Inc., a unit of DuPont Co., and Reading & Bates Corp. said Thursday they had formed a joint venture to run a $400 million deepwater drilling programme in the Gulf of Mexico.
The five-year project was the latest sign of the revitalisation of the offshore drilling industry in the Gulf.

The companies said they had commissioned Korea's Samsung Heavy Industries to build a state-of-the-art $200 million drillship capable of operating in water depths up to 10,000 feet, 2,000 feet deeper than the current drilling record. The ship was set for delivery in 1998.
Conoco President Archie Dunham told reporters at the company's headquarters the drilling project would be "one of the largest in the Gulf of Mexico -- good news for the U.S. petroleum industry."

He said oil experts estimate that 10 billion barrels of oil lie beneath the Gulf's deepwater fields, which are in water at least 1,000 feet deep. The joint venture project will explore in 60 drilling blocks off the coast of Texas and Louisiana.

Dunham said the Gulf of Mexico project was a cornerstone of Conoco's drive to double its current market value of about $15 billion by the year 2003. The company now has 15 million acres in offshore fields worldwide under lease or available for exploration.

Reading & Bates President Paul Lloyd said the 50-50 joint venture "marks the way of the future for oil companies and (drilling) contractors to work together to execute their long-term strategy and achieve a very good financial return while doing so."

The drilling firm's chief financial officer, Tim Nagle, told Reuters the partnership expected cash flow of $215 million from the drillship operations during the five years. Reading & Bates should earn $100 million in net income from the project, he said.

The Gulf of Mexico is in the midst of a drilling boom because of stable oil prices, improved technology and major investments in deepwater fields. Utilization rates for offshore rigs in the Gulf have climbed from 24 percent in 1986 to just over 90 percent, according to industry experts.
Lloyd said the drilling industry is in need of more rigs capable of working in deepwater and predicted the joint venture's ship would be the first of many.
"The fleet to develop these (deepwater) resources hasn't been built yet," he said.
On the New York Stock Exchange, Reading & Bates shares fell $1.125 to $28.75.
